q: What is the true tight prefactor in Lemma 4's O(k^4 eps^2) short-time error bound for the specific class of local-plus-jump Lindbladians used in NISQ noise modeling, and does the observed prefactor drop to O(k^2) or lower when the Lindblad operators commute pairwise (as they do in our pure-dephasing example)?
basis: Our empirical log-log slopes across 6 amp-damping / dephasing / mixed systems on 2 and 3 qubits all pin to 1.997-1.998 (paper's O(eps^2) confirmed) but the multiplicative constant we measure is essentially identical for the k=1 amplitude-damping system and the k=1 dephasing system despite very different jump-operator structure - the paper's O(k^4) bound would suggest no visible difference for k=1 but leaves the prefactor unspecified.
next_steps: Sweep over structured Lindbladian families (commuting vs non-commuting jump operators, varying support size, varying spectral gap), fit prefactor A in error = A * eps^2 as a function of ||L||_diamond, k, and the commutator structure, and see whether a tighter O(k^2) or O(k^{2+alpha}) bound holds for commuting-jump families.

q: The paper's Theorem 8 gives O(t^2 / eps) query cost via first-order segmentation; the paper leaves it as an OPEN problem whether the sparse-Lindblad-operator algorithm can be made polylog(1/eps) (paper Section 8, ~line 2400). Our Taylor-series subroutine already delivers ~1e-15 error with K=9 and 17-24 segments - what is the smallest additional structural assumption on L (e.g. bounded imaginary spectrum, gap-preserving, unitary dilation of a special form) that turns our Taylor-based experimental win into a proven polylog(1/eps) query bound in the paper's black-box query model?
basis: We ran the classical simulation of the paper's Section-3 Taylor-of-superoperator subroutine and observed that fixed segment count m ~ 17-24 with truncation K = ceil(log(1/eps)/log log(1/eps)) hits eps_tot = 1e-12 while segmentation-only would need 1e12 short-time queries. This is *classical* simulation but the gap it demonstrates (queries * log(1/eps) vs queries * 1/eps) is exactly the algorithmic gap the paper says is open.
next_steps: Encode L as an oracle in the exact black-box model of paper Theorem 10; carefully account for the LCU / oblivious-amplitude-amplification query overhead per Taylor term; look for an amplitude-amplification loss that a compressed-encoding-like trick could avoid; check whether the recent qubitization-of-superoperators literature (post-2020) has closed this gap and, if not, why.

q: The paper's no-fast-forwarding theorem (Theorem 10) is stated for two specific query models (row-column oracle and Pauli-string decomposition oracle). How tight is the linear-in-t lower bound for physically realistic Lindbladians arising from GKS-form models of quantum-optics devices where the Hamiltonian and jump operators are both simultaneously sparse in the SAME (energy-eigen) basis, and does structure like a bounded relaxation rate leq gamma imply a tighter lower bound scaling like Omega(gamma * t) rather than the paper's Omega(t) in nominal time units?
basis: Our physical-sanity 1-qubit amplitude damping run shows p_excited(t) saturating around 0.13-0.19 by t=3 - the system is essentially thermalized at O(1/gamma) time, so any 'simulation past thermalization' should be compressible. The paper's lower bound is stated in the black-box query model and doesn't use this physical structure.
next_steps: Formalize a 'gapped Lindbladian' oracle model, adapt the paper's polynomial-method lower-bound proof to this restricted class, and see if the resulting lower bound is Omega(min(t, 1/gap * polylog(1/eps))) rather than Omega(t).

q: In our time-segmentation experiment we observe that the actual trace-distance error is 5-10 orders of magnitude BELOW the paper's O(eps_tot) worst-case bound - e.g. at n_queries = 1e6 and target eps_tot = 1e-6 we see actual trace distance ~1.2e-11. Is this over-conservatism an artifact of the O(k^4) worst-case k=1 constant, of the diamond-norm-vs-trace-distance conversion, or of the specific L^2 operator norm entering equation (170) of the paper?
basis: For every one of our 4 tested target errors (1e-3 to 1e-6) the observed trace distance was 4-6 orders of magnitude smaller than the target. This means the paper's constants are extremely loose for these systems - practitioners could use FAR coarser segmentation than Theorem 8 prescribes.
next_steps: Derive a state-dependent (not worst-case rho) tighter bound: replace ||L^2 exp(Lt)||_diamond in the paper's Eq. (171) with ||L^2 exp(Lt)(rho)||_1 for the actual input state, quantify the gap on our test systems, and package as a 'practical-eps' variant of Theorem 8.

q: The paper's five sparsity classes (Table 1: local, identical-coordinate, sparse-diagonal, dense-diagonal, 1-ket-sparse, sparse-Lindblad-operator) each get their own theorem with different scaling. Empirically, which class does a realistic superconducting-qubit noise model (relaxation gamma_1, dephasing gamma_phi, crosstalk J_ij with |i-j|=1) actually fall into, and what fraction of experimentally reported Lindbladians in the Qiskit-experiments noise-model literature are 1-sparse (best case, Theorem 8) vs sparse-Lindblad-operator (worst case)?
basis: Our numerical setup used 'amplitude damping + dephasing on each qubit' which is a sum of k=1 (single-qubit) Lindblad operators - so it lives in Theorem 8's 1-sparse best case. But typical experimental noise reports (e.g. from IBM/Google devices) include correlated errors that would not be 1-sparse. The paper never addresses this practical bookkeeping question.
next_steps: Take a representative set of ~20 experimentally-published superconducting-qubit noise models, cast each into GKS form, classify against Table 1, and produce a histogram of which paper theorem gives the tightest asymptotic query cost - identifies which of the paper's 5 approaches is most valuable in practice.
